To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

a wide range of tonic depolarizing conductance of GABA does not change the input-output relationship of cortical neurons, whereas a high level of this conductance prevents action potential firing; that a certain range of depolarized GABAergic conductancies can considerably decrease the firing rate of neurons receiving highly fluctuating glutamatergics inputs; and that these results raise the possibility of a sophisticated mechanism of firing rate modulation by GABAAergic inputs with depolarized reversal potentials.

the depolarizing GBAergic inputs do not alter the relationship between the driving conductances and the firing rate of the neuron when the driving inputs are tonic, but do alter it when they are in vivo-like stochastic inputs.

depolarizing Gabaergic inputs can have either no effect or a suppressive effect on the firing rate of cortical neurons driven by in vivo-like fluctuating inputs, depending on the coincidence of GABAergic and excitatory inputs.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the possible effects of depolarized GABAergic inputs in cortical neurons.
the possible role of depolarizing, rather than inhibiting, GABAergic conductive inputs in the modulation of firing rates of cortical pyramidal cells.
the effects of depolarized GABAergic conductive inputs on the neuronal input output relationship.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the depolarizing GBAergic inputs are a sophisticated device for the discriminative firing rate regulation, but not the paradoxical mystery.

a depolarized GABAergic conductace does not affect the relationship between the input driving conductance and output firing rate, but does affect the firing rate of the output neuron in a complex and subtle way, depending on the coincidence between glutametergic and GABAA inputs.
the depolarizing GBAergic inputs are a useful tool for controlling the firing rate of cortical neurons in vivo.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the depolarizing GBAergic inputs are not necessarily harmful, but could be beneficial to cortical information processing.

a neuron driven by highly fluctuating glutamatergigic inputs can be modulated in a wide range of firing rates by a depolarizing GBAergic conductance if a large number (or a large fraction) of the glutamatergically driven inputs are coincident in the presence of the GABAergic inputs.

a depolarized GABAergic conductace may have little effect on the firing rate if glutamatergics are not coincident with it, and may considerably decrease the firing rate if they are coincident with it.
The main takeaway from our work is that
depolarizing Gabaergic inputs can have a profound effect on neuronal output firing rate when they are coincident with glutamatergics.
the depolarization of the GABAA equilibrium potential does not necessarily mean the facilitation of neuronal spiking, but it can also have the opposite effect, depending on the input conditions.

the input-output relationship of a neuron is modulated by depolarizing GABCergic inputs in a complex and context-dependent manner, and thus the effects of GABAergic depolarization should be considered in the interpretation of in vivo experimental results.
